clue.text: Soldier and sailor returning after leave

parts.note: to desert is to leave without permission

indicators.note: something returning comes back the way it went, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: tar is the old slang word for a sailor

explanation.surface: A soldier and a sailor heading back to base once their leave is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' puts the reversed sailor behind the leave word. 'Leave' looks like a noun (shore leave) but works as the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The Desert Rats were the British 7th Armoured Division in North Africa, so any member counts as a soldier.

clue.text: Daughter having too much port

parts.note: D is the standard abbreviation for daughter
over means excessively, as in overdone

explanation.surface: A daughter who has drunk too much port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'port' reads as the fortified wine a daughter has overindulged in; it is really a harbour town.
explanation.definitionFit: Dover is the English Channel ferry harbour in Kent, the classic example of a British seaport.

clue.text: Office suit annoyed by legal proceedings about to be dismissed

indicators.note: someone annoyed is ruffled and disturbed, so these letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: being dismissed means being sent away, so that letter is removed from the word

parts.note: an action is a lawsuit brought in court
C is short for circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: An office worker in a suit is irritated by a lawsuit that is about to be thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged SITU is followed by ACTION with its C dismissed, leaving ATION, to make SITUATION.
explanation.definitionFit: A situation is a job or post, the older sense of an office held by someone, as in 'situations vacant'.

clue.text: Rarely messed up by experts in team events

indicators.note: something messed up has been thrown into disorder, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
aces are people who are expert at something

explanation.surface: Experts in team sports seldom make a mess of things.
explanation.walkthrough: The shuffled RARELY gives RELAYR, then ACES completes RELAY RACES.
explanation.definitionFit: Relay races are contests in which members of a team run consecutive legs, passing a baton between them.

clue.text: Do up shop near the centre of Alfreton

indicators.note: being near something means sitting right beside it, so the two parts are placed next to each other
the centre of a word is its middle, so only the innermost letters are kept

parts.note: the two middle letters of this eight-letter name
a store is a shop

explanation.surface: Refurbishing a shop close to the middle of Alfreton, a small Derbyshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Though the shop is named first, 'near' lets its letters follow those taken from the town.
explanation.definitionFit: To do up an old building or piece of furniture is to restore it, returning it to good condition.

clue.text: Worried teens in court become unable to relax

indicators.note: worried can mean pulled about and harried, so these letters are disturbed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
someone up before the magistrates is in court

explanation.surface: Anxious teenagers appearing in court cannot relax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worried' looks like a description of the teenagers' mood, but it is the signal to rearrange them. Being 'up' in court is short for being up before the judge.
explanation.definitionFit: To tense up is a phrasal verb for growing stiff and anxious, the opposite of loosening or unwinding.

clue.text: Die for soft rugs from the east

indicators.note: in an across answer, coming from the east means reading right to left, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: P is piano, the musical marking for soft
mats are small rugs

explanation.surface: Someone choosing a dye for soft rugs imported from the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Die' suggests dye or death, but it is the tool for stamping metal.
explanation.definitionFit: A die is an engraved block that presses a design into coins or metal, and a stamp is the same impressing tool.

clue.text: Numberless photos of foolish people

indicators.note: numberless means without a number, so the letter that abbreviates number is removed

parts.note: snaps are casual photographs

explanation.surface: Countless snapshots of idiots.
explanation.walkthrough: N is the standard abbreviation for number; take it out of SNAPS to leave SAPS.
explanation.definitionFit: A sap is a gullible, easily fooled person, an informal word for a simpleton or dupe.

clue.text: Specimen not originally large enough

indicators.note: what was there originally is the start, and 'not' removes it, so the first letter goes

parts.note: a sample is a specimen taken for testing

explanation.surface: A lab specimen that turned out to be too small.
explanation.walkthrough: SAMPLE loses its first letter to give AMPLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ample means sufficient or more than enough, so it describes something large enough for the purpose.

clue.text: Game failing to start after concern for winger possibly

indicators.note: failing to start means missing the beginning, so the first letter is dropped
coming after means following behind, so this part is placed second

parts.note: having a part in something is being concerned in it
bridge is a card game

explanation.surface: A sports report: a match fails to kick off after worries about a wide player's fitness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winger' looks like a football wide man, but here it is anything with wings; 'Game' is the card game, not the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A partridge is a game bird, and any bird is a winged creature, hence the 'possibly' marking an example.

clue.text: Girl maintaining it's indispensable

indicators.note: to maintain something is to hold and keep it, so one piece holds another inside

parts.note: Val is a girl's name, short for Valerie
taken as written

explanation.surface: A girl insisting that something cannot be done without.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's' splits into IT plus 's, which stands for 'is' linking wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Vital means essential or absolutely necessary, so a vital thing is one you cannot do without.

clue.text: Breast feeding Polish queen becoming abrasive perhaps

definitions.note: an example of an abrasive; the 'perhaps' signals that

indicators.note: feeding something means putting into it, so one piece goes inside the others

parts.note: to sand a surface is to polish it smooth
pap is an old word for a nipple or breast
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the royal cipher

explanation.surface: A Polish queen nursing a baby who then turns harsh and grating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' is capitalised to suggest the nationality; it is the verb to polish. Pap is an archaic word for a nipple.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandpaper is a sheet coated with grit for smoothing surfaces, one example of an abrasive material.

clue.text: Handy to have tin for cash

parts.note: ready means close at hand, available for use
tin is British slang for money

explanation.surface: It is useful to have a tin of coins to hand for paying cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tin' suggests a cash box, but in British slang tin simply means money.
explanation.definitionFit: Ready money is coins and notes available for immediate payment, the same thing as cash in hand.

clue.text: Suffer when exposed in speech

indicators.note: in speech means as spoken, so we want a word that sounds like another

parts.note: bare means exposed or uncovered

explanation.surface: Someone suffering when their secrets are revealed while they talk.
explanation.walkthrough: BARE (exposed) and BEAR are pronounced identically.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear something is to endure or put up with it, the same sense as to suffer pain or hardship.

clue.text: Head of languages getting extremely upset during squabble with servile flatterer

indicators.note: something happening during another event falls within it, so one piece sits inside

parts.note: to bicker is to squabble over trivia

indicators.note: upset means turned over, and in a down answer that turns the letters upside down
the head of a word is its first letter, which starts this piece

parts.note: first letter of the word
too means excessively, to an extreme degree

explanation.surface: The head of the languages department gets very upset during a staff-room row with a crawler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' looks like the teacher's mood, but in a down answer it turns letters upside down. The squabble word is split open around the turned piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A bootlicker is an informal word for a toady who fawns over superiors, a sycophant who grovels to win favour.

clue.text: Poins is taken in by girl's facial expression of disgust

indicators.note: being taken in by something means being received inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: Grace is a girl's name
Poins is the setter, who would say 'I am', contracted

explanation.surface: The setter is fooled by a girl and makes a face of disgust.
explanation.walkthrough: Poins is this puzzle's setter, and setters refer to themselves by name, so 'Poins is' means 'I am', contracted.
explanation.definitionFit: A grimace is a twisted contortion of the face showing pain, dislike or revulsion.

clue.text: Bravery of girl soldier captured in Lowell's opening lines

indicators.note: something captured is held inside its captor, so one piece is enclosed

parts.note: gal is an informal word for a girl

indicators.note: an opening is a beginning, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of the poet's name
a soldier ant is a caste of ant, so ant stands for soldier
RY is short for railway, and railway lines are the track

explanation.surface: A poem by Robert Lowell opens with the courage of a woman soldier taken prisoner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lines' reads as lines of verse, but it means railway lines. A soldier ant is a caste of ant, so the insect stands in for the soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: Gallantry is courageous conduct, especially in battle, as in medals awarded for gallantry.

clue.text: Went to protect my back in advance

indicators.note: to protect something is to surround and shield it, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: to go is a euphemism for urinating, so went can mean peed

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters run in reverse

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'

explanation.surface: Someone went ahead earlier to guard the speaker's rear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went' and 'my' both pretend to be ordinary words: one is a euphemism for using the toilet, the other an exclamation. 'In advance' hides the definition behind a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To proceed is to go forward or move on, the same as to advance towards something.

clue.text: In distress it's seen by almost everybody as absolutely necessary

indicators.note: something in distress is in a troubled, disordered state, so the letters are thrown about
almost means not quite all, so the last letter is cut

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe
taken as written
all means everybody

explanation.surface: In an emergency, nearly everyone regards something as vital.
explanation.walkthrough: ALL loses its final letter to leave AL, then ITS, SEEN and AL are rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: Essential describes something indispensable that cannot be done without, synonymous with required or vital.

clue.text: Tolerant fellow and striking girl doing a bunk

parts.note: Len is a man's name, short for Leonard

indicators.note: doing a bunk is British slang for running away, so these letters leave the word

parts.note: salient means striking or prominent
Sal is a girl's name, short for Sally

explanation.surface: An easy-going man and a stunning girl run off together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'striking girl' looks like one phrase about a beautiful woman; it is two pieces, with SAL running away from SALIENT to leave IENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Lenient means merciful and permissive, not strict, so a lenient judge is a tolerant one.

clue.text: Rotation is good after shock at home

indicators.note: coming after means placed behind, so this letter goes at the end

parts.note: a turn is a sudden fright, as in 'gave me a turn'
someone at home is in
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A household rota is welcome after a nasty fright at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rotation' suggests a rota of chores, but it means spinning round. A turn as a shock is the British idiom 'it gave me quite a turn'.
explanation.definitionFit: Turning is the act of revolving or spinning about an axis, which is what rotation means.

clue.text: Artist's mother to pose for painters around the London area

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother

indicators.note: turning around means facing the other way, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: a model sits for a portrait painter
SE is the south-east London postcode area

explanation.surface: A painter's mother models for artists somewhere around London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Artist's' reads as possessive, but the 's means 'is'. SE is the London postcode district for the south-east of the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Matisse was the French painter and sculptor who led the Fauvist movement.

clue.text: Ponder over trace of ergot on popular plant

parts.note: to mull over is to ponder

indicators.note: a trace is the smallest hint of something, so only one letter is used

parts.note: first letter of the fungus name
in means fashionable or popular

explanation.surface: A botanist considers signs of ergot fungus on a common plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' belongs with 'Ponder', not as a positional signal. Ergot is a fungal disease of grasses.
explanation.definitionFit: Mullein is a tall flowering herb of the figwort family with woolly leaves and yellow spikes.

clue.text: Supporter finding witty remark after Sunak's first to resign

indicators.note: to resign is to leave a post, so that letter departs from the word

parts.note: a sally is a quick witty retort

indicators.note: first picks out the initial letter of the name

parts.note: initial of the former prime minister's surname

explanation.surface: A backer makes a joke after the prime minister quits.
explanation.walkthrough: Rishi Sunak was the UK prime minister; his initial S leaves SALLY to give ALLY.
explanation.definitionFit: An ally is someone who sides with you and backs your cause, a friend and supporter.

clue.text: Let loose at the outset then relax

indicators.note: the outset is the beginning, so just the first letter is taken

parts.note: first letter of the word
to ease is to relax or loosen

explanation.surface: Let rip at first, then calm down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let loose' looks like a single phrase, but 'Let' is the definition and 'loose' supplies a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To lease a flat or land is to rent it out to a tenant, the property sense of let.

clue.text: Exceptional talent shown by Bill in race abroad

indicators.note: abroad can mean widely scattered, so the letters are spread about anew

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A runner called Bill shows great talent competing overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abroad' suggests a foreign race meeting, but it signals the rearrangement of the three words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Brilliance is outstanding ability or intelligence, so exceptional talent is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Attempt to speak in support of drugs

indicators.note: in a down answer a supporting piece holds up from below, so it is placed second

parts.note: E is ecstasy, so Es are ecstasy tablets
to say is to speak

explanation.surface: Trying to make a public case for drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attempt' looks like a verb, and it is one: ESSAY is a formal verb meaning to try.
explanation.definitionFit: To essay something is a formal verb for trying it, and an essay as a noun is an attempt.

clue.text: Employed by some pious educators

indicators.note: some means part of, so the answer is a portion of the following words

parts.note: letters spanning the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Taken on by devout teachers.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'pioUS EDucators'.
explanation.definitionFit: Employed in the sense of put to use: a tool that has been employed has been utilised.

clue.text: Happen to be right about anger following answer by Penny

indicators.note: following means coming behind, so this piece goes after the others
about can mean turned round, so the letters face the other way

parts.note: RT is an abbreviation for right
ANS is an abbreviation for answer
P is the abbreviation for a penny
ire is anger

explanation.surface: Turning out to be correct about rage that came after a reply from Penny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penny' looks like a woman's name; it is the coin, abbreviated P.
explanation.definitionFit: Transpire is widely used to mean occur or take place, although strictly it means to become known.

clue.text: What Madame Defarge does fools king in the beginning

indicators.note: being in the beginning means standing at the front, so this letter leads

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king
nits are idiots, short for nitwits

explanation.surface: Madame Defarge deceives the king at the start of the Revolution.
explanation.walkthrough: Madame Defarge, in Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities, knits the names of the condemned into her work beside the guillotine.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens shows the revolutionary Madame Defarge constantly knitting, encoding victims' names in stitches.

clue.text: Grant makes a profit

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to concede or give way
second meaning: the return earned on an investment

explanation.walkthrough: 'Grant' looks like a person's name, the subject of 'makes'; it is the verb to concede.
explanation.definitionFit: To yield a point is to concede it, and a yield is the income or return produced by an investment.

clue.text: Officer extremely lucky as a rule

parts.note: a general is a senior army officer

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: An officer who is usually very fortunate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' looks like an intensifier for 'lucky', but it takes only the word's ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Generally means usually or in most cases, so it matches the idiom for what normally happens.
